# Step 3: Upload Your Application to Amazon S3

Step 3 prepares your source content and uploads it to a location from which CodeDeploy can deploy it. The step involves provisioning an Amazon S3 bucket, preparing the revision's files, bundling them, and pushing the revision to the bucket. CodeDeploy can also deploy applications from GitHub repositories to instances, but deploying from GitHub is not covered in this tutorial.

## Create an Amazon S3 bucket

You can create an Amazon S3 bucket or use an existing one. Either way, you can upload the revision to the bucket, and the Amazon EC2 instances used in your deployments can download the revision from it. To create the bucket, you can use the AWS CLI, the Amazon S3 console, or the Amazon S3 APIs. After creating the bucket, you must give access permissions to the bucket and to your AWS account.

Bucket names must be unique across Amazon S3 for all AWS accounts, so you may not be able to use the name amzn-s3-demo-bucket. Use a different name, such as amzn-s3-demo-bucket followed by a dash and your initials or another unique identifier. Wherever amzn-s3-demo-bucket appears in this tutorial, substitute your own bucket name.

Create the bucket in the same AWS Region as your target Amazon EC2 instances; that is, launch the target instances in the same Region as the bucket. With the AWS CLI, the aws s3 mb command creates a bucket. In the S3 console, choose Create bucket, type a bucket name, choose the target Region, and choose Create.

## Grant permissions to the bucket

You must have permissions to upload to the Amazon S3 bucket. You can specify these permissions through an Amazon S3 bucket policy. The example upload policy allows s3:PutObject for AWS account 111122223333 on amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*. The wildcard in this policy allows uploading to any directory in the bucket.

The bucket must also allow download requests from each participating Amazon EC2 instance. You can specify this through an Amazon S3 bucket policy as well. The example download policy allows s3:Get* and s3:List* for the principal role arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo. If an EC2 instance has an attached IAM instance profile containing the role ARN arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo, this policy allows that instance to download files from any directory in the bucket.

## Organize the application files

On the development machine, the WordPress application files, the AppSpec file, and the scripts are organized under /tmp/WordPress. The WordPress folder contains appspec.yml, a scripts folder, wp-admin, wp-content, wp-includes, index.php, license.txt, readme.html, and other .php files. The scripts folder contains change_permissions.sh, create_test_db.sh, install_dependencies.sh, start_server.sh, and stop_server.sh.

## Bundle and push the application

The WordPress application files and the AppSpec file are bundled into an archive file known as an application revision. You may be charged for storing objects in a bucket, and for transferring application revisions into and out of a bucket.

On the development machine, switch to the /tmp/WordPress folder with cd /tmp/WordPress. File bundling starts at the current folder, so if you do not switch to the WordPress folder and instead bundle from /tmp, the bundle includes the files and subfolders in the tmp folder, which may include more than the WordPress subfolder.

The create-application command registers a new application named WordPress_App. The CodeDeploy push command then bundles the files, uploads the revision to Amazon S3, and registers revision information with CodeDeploy in one action. It bundles the files from the current directory into WordPressApp.zip and uploads the revision to the amzn-s3-demo-bucket bucket. The --ignore-hidden-files option excludes hidden files from the bundle.

# Step 3: Upload your application to Amazon S3

## Before you begin

Make sure you have each of the following before starting this step.

- **Permissions for your AWS account to upload to the S3 bucket**, for example through a bucket policy. The steps for setting this up are on this page.
- **An S3 bucket policy that allows your EC2 instances to download revisions from the bucket**, using the instance profile role. The steps are on this page.
- **The IAM instance profile role (CodeDeployDemo) attached to your EC2 instances**, because the bucket policy references it.
- **The WordPress application files, the AppSpec file, and the scripts prepared on your development machine.** The steps are on the linked page.
- **The AWS CLI installed and configured on your development machine**, because the `mb`, `create-application`, and `push` commands use it.

## Overview

This step prepares and uploads source content to a location from which CodeDeploy can deploy it. It involves provisioning an Amazon S3 bucket, preparing the revision's files, bundling them, and pushing the revision to the bucket. CodeDeploy can also deploy applications from GitHub repositories to instances, but deploying from GitHub is not covered in this tutorial.

## Create the Amazon S3 bucket

You can create an Amazon S3 bucket or use an existing bucket. You can upload the revision to the bucket, and the Amazon EC2 instances used in deployments can then download the revision from it. You may be charged for storing objects in a bucket, and for transferring application revisions into and out of a bucket.

You can use the AWS CLI, the Amazon S3 console, or the Amazon S3 APIs to create the bucket. Bucket names must be unique across Amazon S3 for all AWS accounts, so you may not be able to use the name `amzn-s3-demo-bucket`. If that happens, use a different name, such as `amzn-s3-demo-bucket` followed by a dash and your initials or another unique identifier. Then substitute your bucket name for `amzn-s3-demo-bucket` wherever it appears in this tutorial.

Create the bucket in the same AWS Region as your target Amazon EC2 instances. Because the bucket is created in that Region, the instances are launched in the same Region as the bucket, and this holds only when both conditions are met.

To create the bucket with the AWS CLI, use the `aws s3 mb` command. To create it in the S3 console, choose **Create bucket**, type a bucket name, choose the target Region, and choose **Create**.

## Grant permissions to the bucket

You must create the bucket (or choose an existing one) before you can give access permissions to the bucket and your AWS account.

### Upload permissions

You must have permissions to upload to the Amazon S3 bucket. The revision can be uploaded to the bucket only when you hold these permissions. You can specify them through an Amazon S3 bucket policy. The example upload policy allows `s3:PutObject` for AWS account `111122223333` on `amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*`. The wildcard allows uploading to any directory in the bucket, and it does so only because the policy grants that permission on `amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*`.

### Download permissions

The bucket must allow download requests from each participating Amazon EC2 instance. Instances can download the revision from the bucket only when the bucket allows those requests. You can specify download permissions through an Amazon S3 bucket policy. The example download policy allows `s3:Get*` and `s3:List*` for the principal role `arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo`. An EC2 instance has an attached IAM instance profile containing the role ARN `arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo`, so the policy allows such an instance to download files from any directory in the bucket.

## Prepare the application files

The WordPress application files, the AppSpec file, and the scripts are organized on the development machine under `/tmp/WordPress`. The WordPress folder contains `appspec.yml`, a `scripts` folder, `wp-admin`, `wp-content`, `wp-includes`, `index.php`, `license.txt`, `readme.html`, and other `.php` files. The `scripts` folder contains `change_permissions.sh`, `create_test_db.sh`, `install_dependencies.sh`, `start_server.sh`, and `stop_server.sh`.

These files must be organized first. The WordPress application files and the AppSpec file are then bundled into an archive file known as an application revision.

## Bundle and push the revision

On the development machine, switch to the `/tmp/WordPress` folder with `cd /tmp/WordPress`.

If you do not switch to the WordPress folder, bundling starts at the current folder instead. If you bundle from `/tmp`, for example, the bundle includes the files and subfolders in the `tmp` folder, which may include more than the `WordPress` subfolder.

Run the `create-application` command to register a new application named `WordPress_App`.

Then run the CodeDeploy `push` command. In one action, it bundles the files, uploads the revision to Amazon S3, and registers revision information with CodeDeploy. The command bundles the files from the current directory into `WordPressApp.zip`, and it excludes hidden files from the bundle only when the `--ignore-hidden-files` option is used. The bucket must exist and the revision must be ready to upload before the command can upload the revision to the `amzn-s3-demo-bucket` bucket.

**Step 3: Upload your application to Amazon S3**

This step prepares and uploads source content to a location from which CodeDeploy can deploy it. It involves provisioning an Amazon S3 bucket, preparing the revision's files, bundling them, and pushing the revision to the bucket. CodeDeploy can also deploy applications from GitHub repositories to instances, but deploying from GitHub is not covered in this tutorial.

**Create an Amazon S3 bucket**

You can create an Amazon S3 bucket or use an existing one. Either way, you can upload the revision to the bucket, and the Amazon EC2 instances used in deployments can download the revision from it. You can use the AWS CLI, the Amazon S3 console, or the Amazon S3 APIs to create the bucket. After creating it, you must give access permissions to the bucket and to your AWS account.

Bucket names must be unique across Amazon S3 for all AWS accounts, so you may not be able to use the name amzn-s3-demo-bucket. You can use a different name, such as amzn-s3-demo-bucket followed by a dash and your initials or another unique identifier. Wherever amzn-s3-demo-bucket appears in this tutorial, substitute your own bucket name.

Create the bucket in the same AWS Region as your target Amazon EC2 instances, which are launched in the same Region as the bucket. With the AWS CLI, the aws s3 mb command creates a bucket. In the S3 console, choose Create bucket, type a bucket name, choose the target Region, and choose Create.

**Grant permissions to the bucket**

You must have permissions to upload to the Amazon S3 bucket. You can specify these through an Amazon S3 bucket policy. The example upload policy allows s3:PutObject for AWS account 111122223333 on amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*. The wildcard allows uploading to any directory in the bucket.

The bucket must also allow download requests from each participating Amazon EC2 instance. You can specify this through an Amazon S3 bucket policy as well. The example download policy allows s3:Get* and s3:List* for the principal role arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo. If an EC2 instance has an attached IAM instance profile containing the role ARN arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo, this policy allows that instance to download files from any directory in the bucket.

**Organize the application files**

On the development machine, the WordPress application files, the AppSpec file, and the scripts are organized under /tmp/WordPress. The WordPress folder contains appspec.yml, a scripts folder, wp-admin, wp-content, wp-includes, index.php, license.txt, readme.html, and other .php files. The scripts folder contains change_permissions.sh, create_test_db.sh, install_dependencies.sh, start_server.sh, and stop_server.sh.

The WordPress application files and the AppSpec file are bundled into an archive file known as an application revision. Note that you may be charged for storing objects in a bucket, and for transferring application revisions into and out of a bucket.

**Bundle and push the application**

On the development machine, switch to the /tmp/WordPress folder with `cd /tmp/WordPress`. File bundling starts at the current folder, so if you do not switch to the WordPress folder and instead bundle from /tmp, the bundle includes the files and subfolders in the tmp folder, which may include more than the WordPress subfolder.

The create-application command registers a new application named WordPress_App. The CodeDeploy push command then bundles the files, uploads the revision to Amazon S3, and registers revision information with CodeDeploy in one action. It bundles the files from the current directory into WordPressApp.zip, and the --ignore-hidden-files option excludes hidden files from the bundle. The push command uploads the revision to the amzn-s3-demo-bucket bucket.

# Step 3: Upload your application to Amazon S3

## Before you begin

- Application source files, the AppSpec file, and scripts prepared on the development machine (from Step 2). The steps are on the linked Step 2 page.

## Overview

Step 3 prepares and uploads source content to a location from which CodeDeploy can deploy it. The step involves provisioning an Amazon S3 bucket, preparing the revision's files, bundling them, and pushing the revision to the bucket. CodeDeploy can also deploy applications from GitHub repositories to instances, but deploying from GitHub is not covered in this tutorial.

## Create or choose an Amazon S3 bucket

You can create an Amazon S3 bucket or use an existing bucket. You can upload the revision to the bucket, and the Amazon EC2 instances used in deployments can download the revision from the bucket. To create a bucket, you can use the AWS CLI, the Amazon S3 console, or the Amazon S3 APIs. After creating the bucket, you must give access permissions to the bucket and your AWS account, so the bucket must exist before you set those permissions.

Bucket names must be unique across Amazon S3 for all AWS accounts, so you may not be able to use the name amzn-s3-demo-bucket. You can use a different bucket name, such as amzn-s3-demo-bucket followed by a dash and your initials or another unique identifier. Doing so is enough to meet the requirement to substitute your bucket name for amzn-s3-demo-bucket wherever it appears in the tutorial.

Create the bucket in the same AWS Region as the target Amazon EC2 instances. The target instances are launched in the same Region as the bucket only when the bucket has been created in that Region as described, so the two must agree.

To create the bucket with the AWS CLI, use the aws s3 mb command. In the S3 console, choose Create bucket, type a bucket name, choose the target Region, and choose Create.

Note that you may be charged for storing objects in a bucket, and for transferring application revisions into and out of a bucket.

## Grant permissions to the bucket

You can upload the revision to the bucket only when you have permissions to upload to the Amazon S3 bucket. You can specify upload permissions through an Amazon S3 bucket policy. The example upload bucket policy allows s3:PutObject for AWS account 111122223333 on amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*. The wildcard in this example allows uploading to any directory in the bucket, and it does so only because the policy grants that s3:PutObject permission on that resource.

Amazon EC2 instances can download the revision from the bucket only when the bucket allows download requests from each participating instance. You can specify download permissions through an Amazon S3 bucket policy. The example download policy allows s3:Get* and s3:List* for the principal role arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo. An EC2 instance has an attached IAM instance profile containing the role ARN arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/CodeDeployDemo, so the example policy allows such an instance to download files from any directory in the bucket.

## Organize the application files

The WordPress application files, the AppSpec file, and the scripts are organized on the development machine under /tmp/WordPress. This organization must be in place before the files can be bundled into a revision. The WordPress folder contains appspec.yml, a scripts folder, wp-admin, wp-content, wp-includes, index.php, license.txt, readme.html, and other .php files. The scripts folder contains change_permissions.sh, create_test_db.sh, install_dependencies.sh, start_server.sh, and stop_server.sh.

The WordPress application files and the AppSpec file are bundled into an archive file known as an application revision.

## Switch to the WordPress folder and push the revision

On the development machine, switch to the /tmp/WordPress folder with cd /tmp/WordPress. Do this before running the push command. If you do not switch to the WordPress folder, file bundling still starts at the current folder, and bundling from /tmp includes files and subfolders in the tmp folder, which may include more than the WordPress subfolder.

The create-application command registers a new application named WordPress_App.

The CodeDeploy push command bundles the files, uploads the revision to Amazon S3, and registers revision information with CodeDeploy in one action. It bundles the files from the current directory into WordPressApp.zip. The --ignore-hidden-files option excludes hidden files from the bundle, and the bundle excludes them only when that option is used. The push command uploads the revision to the amzn-s3-demo-bucket bucket, so the bucket must already exist and you must have uploaded the revision there with the upload permissions in place.
